title: Chapter 90 – The Fortieth Step
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

On the ninth morning Bai walks him out of the Library in front of everyone.

It is done as he promised, with great ceremony and no explanation. The monk opens the iron door. The old man stands in the stair with his robe brushed and his hair combed, which Jian has never seen, and says in a carrying voice, "The study is concluded. The subject is well. Anyone with an objection may submit it in writing to the Pill Hall, in triplicate." Then he takes Jian's elbow, and the two of them climb the spiral through a silence so thick it seems to have weight.

Disciples line the upper stair. They stand with their backs against the walls and their eyes on the floor, the way people stand when a procession passes that they have been told not to look at. As Jian goes by, he feels them look anyway: a quick glance, a flinch. A boy in the gray of the Outer Sect makes the sign against ill luck behind his sleeve.

At the Library door the daylight is shocking. He lifts a hand against it. The air smells of snow, and wood smoke, and wet stone. In the court beyond, the lanterns are still lit from the night, and under them, at the foot of the steps, stands a ring of men.

Feng is the first he sees.

He is on his feet. It has been a month since the bone-setters wrapped his leg, and he should not be, but he stands in the front rank of the Law Hall guard with his cane hooked on his belt and his gray cloak pinned at the shoulder, and when Jian's eyes find him, he does not look away. He gives one short nod.

Beside him is Tan Ruyan in her silver cloak, with a bodyguard at each elbow. Beside her, in a dark green tunic, stands Wei Chen, long-faced and calm. Zhao Yao is there too, thinner than before, with his hood up and his hands in his sleeves. And behind them all, at a little distance, in a short robe the color of old plums, stands Deputy Rong of the Law Hall with the scale-clerk's ledger under his arm.

Not alone, thinks Jian. Qin Hao said not alone.

He has not asked any of them. He realizes that he did not have to.

"You look dreadful," says Feng, when he reaches the foot of the steps.

"You are standing on a broken leg."

"I am leaning on a cane." Feng's mouth twitches. "It is a distinction I have been developing."

* * *

They climb together, because there is nothing else to do.

It is Bai's idea, or he claims it is, though he claims many things. "The Elders' hall is a trap," he says, as they pass under the Mountain Gate. "Qin Hao said as much to the door, did he not? Then do not walk into it. Walk past it. Let them come to you." He eats a plum. "The Founders' Rule has a clause about it. Any disciple who has reached Foundation under study may, at the study's end, declare for a trial. I looked it up. I even read it."

"Which trial?"

"The one the Sect owes you." The pale eyes crease. "You climbed the Forty Steps as a Qi Refining boy and reported thirty-eight. I do not believe that figure. Neither does the Keeper. Foundation disciples may re-climb. It is an old courtesy, never used."

"You want me to climb."

"I want you to be seen climbing." Bai's voice is mild. "A boy who walks alone into a locked place is a thief. A boy who climbs the Forty Steps in daylight, under the Rule, with a Law Hall deputy and a Pill Hall Elder and half the Inner Court at his back, is a candidate." He pauses. "It is the same boy. It is a different crime."

Jian laughs, despite himself.

They go up the mountain in a long straggling line: the old alchemist with his plums; the tall Feng, using his cane; Tan Ruyan, who has declined to be left behind and is wearing, Jian notices, climbing sandals under the silver cloak; Wei Chen and Zhao Yao, a little apart; the deputy with his ledger. Disciples fall in behind. By the time they reach the first terrace there are sixty of them. By the tenth there are two hundred.

It is not a procession anyone has called. It is a river, and he is a stone dropped in it.

* * *

Elder Mu is waiting at the Founders' Terrace.

He stands in the middle of the path with his arms folded, a wide man with a shaved head and a face that looks as if it has been carved with an ax. His scabbard hangs empty at his hip. Behind him are twelve Law Hall guards in black, with staves crossed, and the sound the crowd makes behind Jian is the sound of two hundred people running out of road.

"This is far enough," says Mu.

"Elder Mu," says Bai. "What a pleasure. Are you taking the air?"

"I am enforcing the Rule." The big man does not look at the alchemist. His eyes are on Jian. "Disciple Lin has been a subject of the Pill Hall's study. The study has ended. By the same Rule, the Law Hall now holds the right to examine a disciple who has undergone an unregistered breakthrough in the Library precincts. I have so determined. He will come with me."

"Examine him how?" asks Feng.

Mu's gaze flicks to him. "Captain Feng. You are on medical leave."

"I am on a cane."

"You are on notice." But there is a hesitation in it. Jian sees it, and sees Mu see him see it. The man's jaw tightens.

"Elder," says Deputy Rong, from the back of the line, in his dry clerk's voice. "A point of procedure."

"Speak."

"The Founders' Rule, section nine, allows a Foundation disciple to declare for the Forty Steps within one day of a study's close. It supersedes the Law Hall's examination for the duration of the climb. I have the section here." He opens his ledger. "Disciple Lin has so declared. I took his declaration at the Library door. You will find my signature, and Elder Bai's, and two witnesses."

"I heard no declaration."

"It was a silent declaration. The Rule does not require a voice." Rong turns a page. "It requires a witness. I was the witness."

For a long moment nobody speaks. A wind comes up the terrace, cold and thin, and stirs the lanterns. Mu's face has gone the dull red of a man doing a sum he does not like.

"This is a farce," he says.

"It is a procedure," says Rong. "I find that the two are often confused."

Jian has not said a word. He stands in the cold with his hands in his sleeves and watches the Elder weigh the Rule against his own anger, and he understands, for the first time, what the Deputy has done. He has not defended Jian. He has made it expensive to stop him.

At last Mu steps aside.

"The climb," he says, in a voice like a closing door. "Then we will see what the Founder's stair makes of you." He looks at Jian a moment longer. "If it breaks you, boy, do not look to me."

"I will not, Elder."

As Jian passes, Mu says very low, so that only he can hear: "There are those who would rather you did not reach the top. I am not among them. I wish you to know I am not among them." His eyes are black and tired. "I would still like to know who is."

* * *

The stair begins at the foot of the Founders' Terrace, and it is exactly as he remembers.

Forty steps of white stone, worn in the middle like a spoon. A railing of black iron. At the top, a landing wide enough for twenty men and, in the far wall, a door. He stops at the bottom with one hand on the rail and looks up.

The last time he stood here he was a boy in an Outer Sect tunic with seven layers of Qi and a lie in his mouth. He climbed thirty-eight steps and stopped, because the stair had pushed back. Now he feels it pushing again: a slow heavy pressure against his chest, like a hand laid flat, patient and weighing. Under it, in the hollow of his sternum, the Seal gives a single warm pulse.

Welcome, it seems to say. You are late.

"Go on," says Bai, from behind.

Before the first step, Feng catches his sleeve.

"A moment."

They stand a little apart from the others, by the first step, with the cold wind between them. Feng has the look of a man who has rehearsed a speech and discarded it. He takes his hand from Jian's sleeve and puts it in his belt.

"I turned my back on that landing once," he says. "At the lock. You asked me to, and I did, and I have thought about it every night since. I did not ask what you were doing. I did not want to know." He looks at the black door above them. "I want to know now."

"I do not have a short answer."

"I did not ask for a short answer."

Jian looks at him. At the cane, the white knuckles, the stubborn jaw. Feng has been wounded for him, and lied for him, and stood on a broken leg in a crowd that would sooner see them both in the Law Hall cells. He has not asked for anything.

"I do not know what is behind it," Jian says. "I know that I was meant to open it. I do not know by whom, or why. I know that there are people in this Sect who would stop me, and that some of them are not the ones I suspect." He takes a breath. "That is all I know. It is not enough."

"It is more than I had." Feng nods slowly. "Go up. If it goes badly, I will hold the stair."

"On that leg?"

"On this leg." The ghost of a grin. "I will lean on the rail. It is a distinction."

He sets his foot on the first step.

The pressure does not increase. That is the first thing he notices. At step ten, where on his last climb the air grew thick, it is as light as the air in the Garden. At step twenty he feels only a faint tingling under the soles of his sandals. At step thirty the stone begins to hum, a long low note, and the iron rail trembles under his palm, and behind him a murmur runs through the crowd like wind in tall grass.

He does not look back.

At thirty-eight he slows, by habit. The place where the stair stopped him is a step like any other, a little more worn at the edge. He puts his foot on it. Nothing happens. He puts his other foot beside it. The stone sighs.

On step thirty-nine, something lies in the middle of the stone.

He nearly puts his foot on it. It is a leaf, small and gray-green, pressed flat against the white as if it had been laid there by hand. Its edge is cut in seven lobes. Around the stem, scratched into the stone with a patient point, is a thin ring.

He stops with one foot raised.

Lan Tong. He knows that ring. He saw it on the leaves in the moon-ash ritual and told no one.

There is no one on the stair to explain it. The nearest disciple is thirty steps below. The mountainside is empty to the cliff. He bends, very slowly, and does not touch it. The leaf is fresh. The ring is fresh. The stone under it is still dusted with the white of a chisel.

He straightens, and steps over it, and does not look back.

Forty.

He stands on the landing.

* * *

The door is lower than he remembered.

It is about the height of a man, and not much wider. It is made of a black stone he cannot name, veined with gray, and set flush into the cliff face with no hinge or handle or seam. Across its face, in three rows, run the marks he saw the first time: cracked, charred, half erased, a lock of some kind. He has looked at them in his mind a hundred times. He has never seen them in daylight.

They are not Sect script.

He sees it now, with Foundation eyes. They are too regular, too small, too like the panels he has read every night of his life. The characters are narrow and square and cut with a perfect economy, as if by a machine. Between them runs a line of smaller marks, bright as embers, and the Seal under his breastbone leans toward them like a plant toward a window.

He reads.

```
ARK-6 / DOCK 2
SEAL: BROKEN (7 of 9 sigils)
TENANT: NONE
ACCESS: HOLDER OF FRAGMENT 3, OR BEARER OF GATE-SEAL + FOUNDATION
```

He stands very still.

It is the Interface's own tongue. It is the same flat clear language that scrolls across his sight each night, cut into a door that has stood on this mountain for six hundred years. It does not look old. It looks new, as though it had been written yesterday and weathered by hands. In the corner of his vision the panel flickers, as it does when it is reading what he is reading.

ARK-6, he thinks. ARK-7 is me.

It is a thought so large that he has no place to put it. He sets it aside, carefully, as one sets aside a full cup, and keeps walking.

"Lin Jian."

It is Qin Hao.

The Elder has come up the stair behind him, silent as smoke. He stands on the topmost step in his plum robe with his hands folded, and behind him, on the stair, stand the others: Mu of the Law Hall with a bare sheath at his hip; Zhou of the Treasury, small and round-faced and anxious; a gaunt white-haired woman in the gray of the Sutra Hall whom Jian has never seen; three more he does not know. A silence has fallen over the whole mountainside.

"Disciple Lin," says Qin Hao. "You are at the door."

"Yes, Elder."

"It has not opened in six hundred years." The dry voice does not rise. "No disciple has tried it in four hundred. The last was a Foundation cultivator of great merit. He did not return."

"I know."

"Do you?" A pause. "Then you know that I must ask you what you intend."

Jian turns.

He faces them across the landing: the Elders, the guard, the silver cloak and the indigo one, the old man with his plum, the tall boy with his cane. Below them the crowd fills the stair to the bottom and spills out across the terrace, faces upturned, breath white in the cold. Two hundred pairs of eyes. More. He had not known there were so many.

I could lie, he thinks. I could say I came to look.

It would be the sensible thing. It would be what he has done all year.

"I intend to open it," he says.

* * *

He lays his hand on the door.

It is warm. That is the second surprise. The stone is cold as a grave in the shadow of the cliff, but under his palm it has a living heat, the heat of a body, and when he presses, the cracked marks glow.

Seal: detected, says the panel.

The Seal in his chest answers. It is a deep slow chord that goes through his ribs and out through his hand and into the stone, and the stone replies. He feels the door waking. He feels, very distinctly, an enormous quiet machine under the mountain turn over in its sleep.

"Stand back," someone says, behind him. It is Feng. His voice is quite steady.

He does not need to be told. The Qi sense, which has been silent for days, floods out of him like a spring. He feels the landing, the stair, the people on it, two hundred small flames and a few big ones. He feels the cliff. He feels the door, a vast dense cold weight that goes down and down into the heart of the rock. And he feels a thing he has no word for, a presence on the other side, a patient listening.

Foundation, says the panel. Gate-Seal. Verify.

```
VERIFY: Foundation Establishment (Early) ... OK
VERIFY: Gate-Seal (strained, 91% recovered) ... OK
VERIFY: Bearer identity ... UNKNOWN
Prior bearer record: NONE.
Proceed on provisional access? [Y / N]
CE: 6.
```

Provisional. He reads the word with a small cold shock. The door does not know who he is. It has no record of him. It will let him in because he carries the key, not because he has the right.

He thinks of the Founder's nine-year-old disciple, and the pill never taken. He thinks of Heng, in his cold cell, who said the door was older than the Sect and asked for one favor in return. The favor is not yet due. It feels, all the same, as if it were.

He presses Y.

The door opens.

It does not swing. It does not slide. It unfolds, panel by panel, in a series of soft clicks, folding in on itself like a flower going back to bud, until there is a dark opening in the cliff the height of a man. A breath of air comes out of it. It is cold and dry and smells faintly of metal, and of something else, something he has not smelled since the cradle: the clean sharp scent of a room where machines have been running for a very long time.

Behind him, a woman screams.

It is not a scream of fear. It is the sound of someone who has seen a thing she has read about all her life and never believed. Somewhere on the stair, an old man begins to laugh, high and cracked, and does not stop. Elder Zhou has sat down on the top step with his hand over his mouth. The gaunt woman from the Sutra Hall has gone white as paper and is saying, over and over, in a whisper, the Gate. The Gate. The Gate is open.

And then the bell begins.

It is not the Library bell. It is the great bell on the Mountain Gate, the one that has not rung since the Founder's day, and it rings now without a hand, in slow thunderous strokes that shake the cliff. Every disciple on the mountainside hears it. Every Elder, every servant, every bird on the roof. In the valley below, in the Medicine Garden and the market town and the Gray Peak mines, men stop what they are doing and lift their heads.

The Sect knows, thinks Jian.

He has no illusion about it. He could not have kept it secret if he had wanted to. He opened the door in daylight with two hundred witnesses, and whatever else he may be, he is now a boy who has done what the Founders' register says no one living can do. There is a cost to that. There is always a cost. He feels it settle on his shoulders like a cloak, heavy and wet.

Then, at the very back of the crowd, he feels it.

It is a single flame, cold and thin, as steady as a pinned candle. It stands apart from the rest. It does not move when the bell rings. It does not flinch when the woman screams. He turns his head by the smallest degree and looks, and under a dead pine beside the stair, stands a figure in a gray hooded cloak with its face in shadow.

The figure raises an open palm.

It is not a greeting. It is not a threat. It is the gesture of a man holding up a hand to show that it is empty. He has seen it once before, in the Wellmaster's cellar, and it meant nothing then. It means something now.

Jian does not look away. He fixes the shape in his mind: the height, the stoop, the way the left shoulder rides a little higher than the right.

The palm lowers. The hood turns. By the time Jian blinks, the pine is empty.

He turns to Qin Hao.

The old Elder has not moved. He stands in his plum robe at the head of the stair with his hands folded and his face gone slack and gray. He is looking past Jian into the dark. His lips move.

"Elder?" says Jian.

"I did not believe it," says Qin Hao.

It is very quiet. It is the voice of a man who has been carrying a weight so long that he has forgotten it was a weight, and has just been told to put it down.

"I did not believe a word of it." He lifts his eyes. "Go in, Disciple Lin. Go in before I change my mind."

Jian looks at Feng, who nods. He looks at Tan Ruyan, who has her hand pressed flat against her silver cloak, over her heart, and is not breathing. He looks at Bai, who has stopped eating his plum.

He steps through the door.

* * *

The air inside is warmer than he expected.

The passage runs ahead of him for perhaps ten paces, a square tunnel of smooth gray stone lit by a thin white line along the ceiling. There are no torches. There is no source of light that he can see, only a pale steady glow that makes his shadow stand out sharp and black on the floor. The walls are lined with panels of the same black stone as the door, each cut with rows of tiny square marks, all dark.

Then the passage ends and the floor falls away.

He stops at the edge. It is not a pit. It is a stair: a broad shallow flight of steps cut straight down into the mountain, wide enough for ten men, so long that its bottom is lost in a blue haze. The steps are white. They glimmer. Every one of them is lined along its edge with that thin line of light, and the lines converge, as they descend, into a single point of brightness far below.

He counts without meaning to. Forty. Eighty. A hundred.

It goes down, he thinks. It goes down into the mountain.

Behind him, at the entrance, he hears the crowd draw breath. He hears Feng's voice, low and urgent, telling the Law Hall guard to hold the line. He hears Bai say something to Qin Hao, and Qin Hao say something back. He hears Pebble, on his shoulder, make a small startled sound.

Cold, says Pebble. Metal. Old. Old, old.

The panel flickers at the edge of his sight.

```
ARK-6 / DOCK 2: ONLINE (partial).
Life support: 4%.
Fabricator: DORMANT.
Bench: AWAITING OPERATOR.
Welcome, Operator.
```

He does not move.

The word hangs there in the bright air. Operator. It is not what the cradle called him. It is not Gardener. It is something older, something that has been waiting for six hundred years for someone to read it, and the Seal in his chest has begun to beat in time with the lights.

Who built this? he thinks.

The stair does not answer.

He puts his foot on the first step down.
